title: Partial Index Concept
description: Reason about predicate coverage, subset transitions and active-only uniqueness, while distinguishing PostgreSQL partial indexes from MySQL alternatives and plan assumptions.

questions.question_text: What is a partial index?
options: An index that only stores half of each row's data
An index that covers only a subset of a table's rows matching a specified condition
An index that is deleted automatically after a week
An index that can only be built on numeric columns
questions.explanation: A partial (filtered) index restricts its entries to rows that satisfy a WHERE condition, rather than covering the entire table.

questions.question_text: Which SQL dialect has NO native support for partial/filtered indexes?
options: PostgreSQL
SQL Server
MySQL
All of the above lack support
questions.explanation: MySQL has no native partial/filtered index feature, unlike PostgreSQL (WHERE clause on CREATE INDEX) and SQL Server (filtered indexes).

questions.question_text: What is the main benefit of a partial index over a full index on the same column?
options: It stores every row twice
It can be smaller and reduce eligible access or maintenance work, but benefits depend on subset, queries and transitions
It always eliminates all writes
It is guaranteed faster for every workload
questions.explanation: The subset can reduce work, but no universal speed or maintenance guarantee follows.

questions.question_text: A partial index is built with `WHERE status = 'pending'`. Can it help a query filtering `WHERE status = 'completed'`?
options: Yes, partial indexes cover all possible values regardless of condition
No, since 'completed' rows were never included in this partial index
Yes, but only for status values starting with 'p'
It depends only on the table's clustered index
questions.explanation: A partial index only contains entries for rows matching its defining condition; rows outside that condition simply aren't indexed at all.

questions.question_text: What is a common real-world use case for combining a partial index with a uniqueness rule?
options: Enforcing global uniqueness across every row in the table, always
Enforcing uniqueness only among 'active' (non-soft-deleted) rows, e.g., UNIQUE(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
Preventing any INSERT statements from ever running
Making every column in the table NOT NULL
questions.explanation: A very common pattern is a partial unique index that enforces uniqueness only among active rows, allowing reused values among soft-deleted rows.

questions.question_text: Why does a partial index reduce write overhead compared to a full index on the same column?
options: Every write becomes free
Rows remaining excluded can avoid member-entry maintenance, but predicate-changing updates can enter or leave the index
It disables transaction logging
Only SELECT statements remain legal
questions.explanation: A previously nonmatching row can become a member. Predicate evaluation and exact engine maintenance still matter.

questions.question_text: What happens if application query patterns shift so that the partial index's condition no longer matches common queries?
options: The database throws a fatal error
The partial index quietly stops being useful/chosen by the optimizer, without any error
The partial index automatically updates its own condition
All queries against the table stop working
questions.explanation: A partial index simply becomes irrelevant to new query patterns silently; there's no automatic detection or alert for this.

questions.question_text: In PostgreSQL, how is a partial index typically defined?
options: Using a WHERE clause appended to CREATE INDEX
Using a special PARTIAL keyword before INDEX
By creating two separate tables
Partial indexes cannot be defined via SQL syntax at all
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL supports partial indexes natively via a WHERE clause at the end of the CREATE INDEX statement.

questions.question_text: What does a partial-index predicate control?
options: Which base rows have entries in that index
Which rows are deleted from the table
Which users authenticate
The final result ordering automatically
questions.explanation: Excluded rows remain in the base relation.

questions.question_text: Does pending-or-completed imply a pending-only index predicate?
options: Yes, both are statuses
No
Only if ordered
Only when the table is small
questions.explanation: The query includes rows the partial index excludes.

questions.question_text: What can a generic prepared plan lack?
options: Permission to bind values safely
Proof that a variable status parameter always means pending
Any query syntax
Every table statistic
questions.explanation: Planner eligibility depends on information available at plan time.

questions.question_text: What happens when a completed row becomes pending?
options: It must remain excluded forever
It deletes the table
It can enter the partial index
It commits every transaction
questions.explanation: Membership is maintained as predicate values change.

questions.question_text: Does a partial unique active-email index imply unconditional historical email uniqueness?
options: Yes, all rows are included
Only if email is text
Only after a refresh
No
questions.explanation: Uniqueness applies to the indexed subset under its comparison semantics.

questions.question_text: Can reactivating a soft-deleted record fail?
options: Yes, if it conflicts with another active indexed identity
No, reactivation bypasses uniqueness
Only after an application restart
Only with a short email
questions.explanation: The row reenters the constrained subset.

questions.question_text: Does the example automatically make email case-insensitive?
options: Yes, all indexes lowercase strings
No
Only if deleted_at is NULL
Only in a small table
questions.explanation: Collation and normalization are distinct design decisions.

questions.question_text: Does PostgreSQL-style CREATE INDEX WHERE run unchanged on MySQL 8.4?
options: Yes, universally
Only with one key
No
Only for pending rows
questions.explanation: Native feature syntax differs across engines.

questions.question_text: Is a full MySQL status-key composite index physically identical to a partial index?
options: Yes, it omits excluded rows automatically
Only if named partial
Only if UNIQUE is absent
No
questions.explanation: It stores a different population despite possibly helping similar lookups.

questions.question_text: What should a maintenance benchmark include?
options: Rows entering and leaving the predicate subset
Only a static read screenshot
Only creation time
Only column count
questions.explanation: Predicate-changing writes can add or remove member entries.

questions.question_text: Can a valid partial index become less useful after workload change?
options: No, it guarantees every future plan
Yes
Only after corruption
Only when renamed
questions.explanation: Validity and workload usefulness are separate properties.

questions.question_text: Where should concurrent active-identity conflict be verified?
options: Only in a disabled UI button
Only in an application precheck
At actual database enforcement with allowed and denied cases
Only by counting captions
questions.explanation: A precheck can race; the trusted unique rule must arbitrate.

notes:
## Index a defined subset rather than every row

A partial index contains entries only for table rows satisfying an index predicate. It can focus an access path or a uniqueness rule on a meaningful subset, such as pending workshop requests or active records not marked deleted. The predicate determines membership in the index. It does not remove excluded rows from the base table or prevent other queries from reading them through authorized access paths.

The feature is engine-specific. PostgreSQL supports predicate indexes, and SQL Server has a related filtered-index feature with its own restrictions. MySQL 8.4 does not offer the same native CREATE INDEX with a row-filtering WHERE clause. A PostgreSQL example should therefore be labeled explicitly rather than submitted unchanged to a MySQL-oriented judge. Conceptual alternatives can have different storage and enforcement behavior.

## Start with a pending-work lookup

Suppose a service retains millions of completed requests but regularly retrieves a small pending population by workshop identifier. An index restricted to pending rows can be smaller than a full index on the same key. It can reduce work for eligible queries and some maintenance operations, while still needing predicate evaluation and membership changes. The benefit depends on the actual subset size, query frequency and write pattern.

```sql
-- PostgreSQL syntax;not MySQL8.4:
CREATE INDEX pending_request_workshop_idx
ON workshop_requests(workshop_id,request_id)
WHERE status='pending';
```

A query with WHERE status='pending' AND workshop_id=7 is a candidate for this access path. A query requiring every completed request cannot obtain that excluded population from the partial index alone. The optimizer may choose another index or a table scan. Creating an index establishes an available structure, not a guarantee that every eligible query will select it.

## Prove that the query implies the index predicate

An optimizer can use a partial index for a query only when it can establish that the relevant query population is covered by the index. A query explicitly requiring pending status implies the example predicate. A query requiring status pending or completed does not. The index lacks completed entries, so treating it as the complete source would silently miss required rows.

Mathematical implication and planner recognition are related but different requirements. A complicated logically equivalent expression may not be recognized by a particular planner. PostgreSQL's documentation describes limited implication recognition rather than a general theorem prover. Align query predicates with the intended index contract and inspect the actual plan. Do not assume every algebraically clever rewrite preserves an optimizer's ability to prove eligibility.

Prepared statements add another consideration. A generic plan whose status parameter could take several values cannot assume the parameter always means pending. A concrete custom plan can have different information. Test the installed driver's preparation and planning behavior instead of claiming that all parameterized queries always use, or never use, the index. Correct value binding must not be abandoned merely to chase an access path.

## Trace rows entering and leaving the subset

An inserted pending request needs a partial-index entry. An inserted completed request does not need an entry in that pending-only structure. Updating a completed request to pending can create an entry; updating pending to completed can remove one. Updating an indexed key on a qualifying row can modify its entry. Predicate membership is therefore part of index maintenance, not a condition checked only at creation time.

| Change | Before membership | After membership | Index consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Insert pending | No row | Included | Add entry |
| Insert completed | No row | Excluded | No member entry |
| Pending to completed | Included | Excluded | Remove entry |
| Completed to pending | Excluded | Included | Add entry |

It is too strong to say a write to a currently excluded row can never touch the index. A predicate-changing update can move that row into the subset, and the engine may also evaluate membership during maintenance. A nonqualifying row that remains nonqualifying may avoid member-entry work, but exact implementation cost still needs measurement. Include status transitions in any claimed maintenance benchmark.

## Enforce uniqueness only where the rule applies

A partial unique index can express one-active-record rules. For example, a system can permit several archived contact records sharing an email while requiring at most one active record for that email under the declared comparison semantics. The predicate identifies active rows; the indexed key defines which active values conflict. The rule is narrower than unconditional email uniqueness across every historical record.

```sql
-- PostgreSQL example for an explicitly defined active-record rule:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX active_contact_email_uq
ON contact_records(email)
WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;
```

A second active row with a conflicting nonnull email should fail under this rule. Multiple excluded historical rows are not members of that unique subset. NULL treatment, collation and case normalization require separate decisions; the example does not automatically implement case-insensitive uniqueness or forbid every nullable email. State the exact domain and comparison rule before treating the index as a complete identity policy.

## Test reactivation and concurrent conflicts

Soft deletion changes subset membership. Reactivating an archived record can fail if another active record now uses the same indexed email. That is an intended enforcement outcome, not a reason to weaken the rule during restoration. A trusted workflow must report or reconcile the conflict without revealing another user's private record or silently changing the identifier.

Two concurrent attempts to create the same active identity must be tested at the database enforcement point. A client-side check that no active record exists can race with another request. The unique rule arbitrates the actual conflict, while application handling maps the result into the intended business response. Test permitted historical duplication, denied active duplication and denied reactivation with the actual engine and actor permissions.

## Distinguish MySQL alternatives without inventing equivalence

A regular composite MySQL index beginning with status can support useful pending lookups, but it still indexes a different population and has different storage characteristics. Generated-column or functional-index patterns can sometimes help express a selected uniqueness rule using NULL behavior, subject to engine restrictions and exact expressions. Those patterns are not native partial indexes merely because they target a similar business requirement.

Do not copy the PostgreSQL WHERE clause onto MySQL CREATE INDEX and assume the server will silently emulate it. Nor should an educational comparison modify a real application's indexes or generated columns without reviewed schema approval. The lesson prepares access-path and constraint reasoning; operational changes require a verified existing schema, callers, rollback plan and suitable database tests.

## Evaluate a changing workload

A pending-only structure is most attractive when pending rows remain a suitably small useful subset. If nearly every request becomes pending, the size advantage can shrink. If the dominant queries shift to completed history, the structure can remain valid while contributing little. Monitor actual plans, subset distribution and write cost rather than equating successful index creation with permanent usefulness.

Avoid creating a separate partial index for every conceivable category without evidence. Many overlapping structures add maintenance and planning complexity, and a partitioning requirement is a different design question. Compare a small set of justified alternatives on representative data. Preserve the required result population and uniqueness semantics while measuring performance; an incomplete query is not a valid faster version of a complete one.

Record the exact predicate text, comparison types and parameter values alongside any plan observation. A later query rewrite or driver planning change can alter eligibility without changing the business-facing screen. Retesting those conditions is more informative than assuming that an old successful benchmark establishes every future prepared execution.

## Solve two predicate-membership exercises

First exercise: classify queries for pending workshop 7, completed workshop 7, and all statuses workshop 7 against the pending-only index. Only the first query population is fully covered under the stated predicate. Then update a completed row to pending and explain why an entry is added. The result comes from implication and membership, not a claim that a plan has been executed.

Second exercise: insert one active email record and two archived copies, then attempt another active row and a conflicting reactivation in an isolated PostgreSQL lab. The solution permits the archived duplicates and rejects the active conflicts under the specified nonnull email rule. Continue with [unique indexes](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/unique-index), [function-based index concepts](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/function-based-index-concept) and [index maintenance](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/index-maintenance) to compare supported mechanisms without erasing engine boundaries.
